title: حِكَايَةُ قَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 836–837 (Night 185, continuing nights-184), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 185 continues the tale of Qamar al-Zamān. Queen Budūr, seized by love for the stranger asleep beside her, reproaches herself, then wishes she had known he was the suitor her father put to her, and tries to wake him; but Maymūna lets sleep down over him and he does not stir. Budūr pleads, coaxes and scolds, suspecting that her father has forbidden him to speak to her, and then finds her own ring on his little finger. She opens his shirt, kisses him and runs her hand over his body down to his penis, and desire surges in her, for, the narrator says, women's desire is stronger than men's. She takes his ring in exchange for hers, kisses him all over, and sleeps holding him in her arms. Dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْخَامِسَةُ وَالثَّمَانُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-khāmisatu wa-al-thamānūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the fifth and-the-eighty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eighty-fifth night,
sentences.n: al-khāmisa, “the fifth”, agrees with al-layla, and the tens, al-thamānūna, follow in the same nominative case. The ئ of المائة is printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ الْمَلِكَةَ بُدُورَ لَمَّا رَأَتْ قَمَرَ الزَّمَانِ أَخَذَهَا الْهُيَامُ وَالْوَجْدُ وَالْغَرَامُ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-malikata Budūra lammā raʾat Qamara al-Zamāni akhadhahā al-huyāmu wa-al-wajdu wa-al-gharāmu
sentences.l: She-said: It-has-reached-me, O fortunate king, that the-Queen Budūr, when she-saw Qamar al-Zamān, took-her the-love-madness and-the-longing and-the-passion.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when Queen Budūr saw Qamar al-Zamān, she was seized by love-madness, longing and passion.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the story by repeating the last sentence of the previous night. The print runs السعيد and ان together as one word, السعيدان; the spacing is kept, and the pair is read al-saʿīdu anna. anna puts al-malikata in the accusative, and the sentence restarts after lammā: akhadhahā, “(they) seized her”, with the three feelings as subject. huyām and gharām rhyme in -ām, in the manner of rhymed prose. رأت has its hamza printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ فِي نَفْسِهَا وَافَضِيحَتَاهْ إِنَّ هٰذَ اشَابٌّ غَرِيبٌ لَا أَعْرِفُهُ مَابَالُهُ رَاقِدًا بِجَنْبِي فِي فِرَاشٍ وَاحِدٍ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat fī nafsihā wā-faḍīḥatāh inna hādhā shābbun gharībun lā aʿrifuhu mā bāluhu rāqidan bi-janbī fī firāshin wāḥidin
sentences.l: And-she-said in herself: O-disgrace! Indeed this (is) a-young-man, a-stranger, I-do-not-know-him; what (is) his-case, lying at-my-side in one bed?
sentences.i: And she said to herself, “Oh, the shame of it! This is a young man, a stranger I do not know. What is he doing, lying beside me in the same bed?”
sentences.n: qālat fī nafsihā, “she said in herself”, that is, to herself. wā-faḍīḥatāh, “oh, the disgrace!”: wā, the particle of lament, with the ending -āh that closes such a cry. The print sets هذ اشاب: the alif that ends hādhā has drifted onto the next word. The spacing is kept, and the phrase is read inna hādhā shābbun, “this is a young man”, with hādhā as the subject of inna (it shows no case) and shābbun as its predicate. lā aʿrifuhu, “I do not know him”, describes the stranger without a relative pronoun, as usual after an indefinite noun. mā bāluhu, “what is his case?”, is printed as one word, ماباله: bāl, “state, concern”. rāqidan, “lying”, is a circumstantial accusative: “what is the matter with him, lying …?”. bi-janbī, “at my side”: bi- of place, with janb, “side”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَتْ إِلَيْهِ ثَانِيَ مَرَّةٍ وَتَأَمَّلَتْ حُسْنَهُ وَجَمَالَهُ فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ إِنَّهُ شَابٌّ مَلِيحٌ إِلَّا أَنَّ كَبِدِي تَكَادُ أَنْ تَتَمَزَّقَ وَجْدًا عَلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma naẓarat ilayhi thāniya marratin wa-taʾammalat ḥusnahu wa-jamālahu fa-qālat wa-Allāhi innahu shābbun malīḥun illā anna kabidī takādu an tatamazzaqa wajdan ʿalayhi
sentences.l: Then she-looked at-him a-second time and-contemplated his-beauty and-his-loveliness, and-said: By-God, indeed-he (is) a-young-man handsome; except that my-liver is-about to be-torn-apart (with) longing for-him.
sentences.i: Then she looked at him a second time and gazed long on his beauty and loveliness, and said, “By God, he is a handsome young man; but my heart is all but torn to pieces with longing for him.
sentences.n: thāniya marratin, “a second time”: an adverbial accusative, the ordinal in construct with marra, “time”, a usual order in later Arabic. taʾammala, Form V, “to gaze long at, contemplate”; the shadda of وتامّلت is the print's own. wa-Allāhi, “by God”: wa- of the oath, with the genitive. illā anna, “except that”, here simply “but”. kabid, “liver”, is feminine, and for Arabic it is a seat of the passions where English says “heart”. kāda, “to be on the point of”, here takes an and the subjunctive, takādu an tatamazzaqa; the grammarians prefer it without an, but the construction is common. tamazzaqa, Form V, “to be torn to shreds”. wajdan, “from longing”, an accusative of cause; ʿalā marks the one longed for.

sentences.t: فَيَا فَضِيحَتِي مِنْهُ وَاللَّهِ لَوْ عَلِمْتُ أَنَّ هٰذَا الشَّابَّ هُوَ الَّذِي خَطَبَنِي مِنْ أَبِي مَا رَدَدْتُهُ بَلْ كُنْتُ أَتَزَوَّجُهُ وَأَتَمَلَّى بِجَمَالِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-yā faḍīḥatī minhu wa-Allāhi law ʿalimtu anna hādhā al-shābba huwa alladhī khaṭabanī min abī mā radadtuhu bal kuntu atazawwajuhu wa-atamallā bi-jamālihi
sentences.l: So-O my-disgrace from-him! By-God, if I-had-known that this the-young-man, he (is) the-one-who asked-for-me from my-father, not I-would-have-refused-him; rather I-would-be marrying-him and-taking-my-fill with-his-beauty.
sentences.i: Oh, the shame he brings on me! By God, had I known that this young man was the one who asked my father for my hand, I would not have refused him; I would have married him and taken my fill of his beauty.”
sentences.n: fa-yā faḍīḥatī minhu, “O my disgrace from him!”: yā calls no one here and is a cry, and min gives the cause, the shame he brings her. law … mā radadtuhu, “if I had known … I would not have refused him”: law takes a perfect in both halves of an unreal condition, and the answer is negated with mā. huwa alladhī, “(he is) the one who”: the pronoun marks off the predicate. khaṭaba (a girl) min abīhā, “to ask her father for her hand”: min marks the one asked. Budūr has refused every suitor her father put before her, and she wonders whether this was one of them. bal kuntu atazawwajuhu, “rather I would have married him”: kuntu with an imperfect, here the answer to law. tamallā bi-, Form V, “to take one's fill of”: bi- marks what is enjoyed. The shaddas of اتزوّجه and واتملّى are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَظَرَتْ إِلَى وَجْهِهِ وَقَالَتْ يَا سَيِّدِي وَنُورَ عَيْنِي انْتَبِهْ مِنَ النَّوْمِ وَتَمَتَّعْ بِحُسْنِي وَجَمَالِي
sentences.tr: thumma naẓarat ilā wajhihi wa-qālat yā sayyidī wa-nūra ʿaynī intabih mina al-nawmi wa-tamattaʿ bi-ḥusnī wa-jamālī
sentences.l: Then she-looked at his-face and-said: O my-master and-light (of) my-eye, wake from the-sleep and-enjoy with-my-beauty and-my-loveliness.
sentences.i: Then she looked into his face and said, “My lord, light of my eye, wake from your sleep and take your pleasure of my beauty and loveliness.”
sentences.n: nūra ʿaynī, “light of my eye”, is still governed by the yā: a noun in construct is accusative after the vocative. intabih, imperative of intabaha, Form VIII, “to wake”. tamattaʿa bi-, Form V, “to enjoy”: bi- marks what is enjoyed; the shadda of وتمتّع is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ حَرَّكَتْهُ بِيَدِهَا فَأَرْخَتْ عَلَيْهِ مَيْمُونَةُ الْجِنِّيَّةُ النَّوْمَ وَثَقُلَتْ عَلَى رَأْسِهِ بِجَنَاحِهَا فَلَمْ يَسْتَيْقِظْ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ
sentences.tr: thumma ḥarrakathu bi-yadihā fa-arkhat ʿalayhi Maymūnatu al-jinniyyatu al-nawma wa-thaqulat ʿalā raʾsihi bi-janāḥihā fa-lam yastayqiẓ Qamaru al-Zamāni
sentences.l: Then she-moved-him with-her-hand; and-let-down over-him Maymūna the-jinniyya the-sleep, and-lay-heavy upon his-head with-her-wing; so-not woke Qamar al-Zamān.
sentences.i: Then she stirred him with her hand; but Maymūna the jinniyya let sleep down over him and weighed on his head with her wing, and Qamar al-Zamān did not wake.
sentences.n: The jinn are still watching unseen. It is Budūr's turn to wake and find the other sleeper, and Maymūna, who backs Qamar al-Zamān, keeps him asleep. arkhā, Form IV, “to let down, let hang”, as one lets down a curtain: arkhat ʿalayhi al-nawma, “she let sleep down over him”. wa-thaqulat ʿalā raʾsihi, “and she lay heavy on his head”: thaqula ʿalā, “to be heavy upon”. The letters also allow Form II, thaqqalat, “she weighed (it) down”, to the same effect. The hamza of رأسه is printed. istayqaẓa, Form X, “to wake”, jussive after lam.

sentences.t: فَصَارَتِ الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ تَهُزُّهُ بِيَدِهَا وَتَقُولُ لَهُ بِحَيٰوتِي عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تُطِيعَنِي
sentences.tr: fa-ṣārati al-malikatu Budūru tahuzzuhu bi-yadihā wa-taqūlu lahu bi-ḥayātī ʿalayka an tuṭīʿanī
sentences.l: So-began the-Queen Budūr shaking-him with-her-hand and-saying to-him: By-my-life upon-you, that you-obey-me!
sentences.i: So Queen Budūr began to shake him with her hand, saying, “By my life, I beg you, do as I ask:
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin to, set about”; the shadda of تهزّه is the print's own. بحيوتي is bi-ḥayātī, “by my life”, with ḥayāt in its old spelling with wāw, like حيوة; the dagger alif shows the long ā. bi- is the bi- of adjuring, “by”, and ʿalayka, “upon you”, lays the oath on the one addressed: “I adjure you by my life”. an tuṭīʿanī, “that you obey me”, depends on the adjuration: “(I adjure you) to obey me”.

sentences.t: فَانْتَبِهْ مِنْ مَنَامِكَ وَانْظُرْإِلَى النَّرْجِسِ وَالْخُضْرَةِ وَتَمَتَّعْ بِبَطْنِي وَالسُّرَّةِ وَهَارِشْنِي وَنَاغِشْنِى مِنْ هٰذَا الْوَقْتِ إِلَى بُكْرَةْ
sentences.tr: fa-intabih min manāmika wa-unẓur ilā al-narjisi wa-al-khuḍrati wa-tamattaʿ bi-baṭnī wa-al-surrati wa-hārishnī wa-nāghishnī min hādhā al-waqti ilā bukra
sentences.l: so-wake from your-sleep and-look at the-narcissus and-the-greenness, and-enjoy with-my-belly and-the-navel, and-romp-with-me and-dally-with-me from this the-time until tomorrow.
sentences.i: wake from your sleep and look on the narcissus and the green, take your pleasure of my belly and my navel, romp with me and play with me from this hour until tomorrow.
sentences.n: The print has وانطرالى, a misprint for وانظرالى, corrected here: wa-unẓur ilā, “and look at”, the dot of the ẓāʾ having dropped. The print's spacing, with the two words set as one, is kept. manām, “sleep”, a verbal noun of nāma. The narcissus, narjis, is the stock image of love poetry for the languid eye: she offers him her eyes. al-khuḍra, “greenness”, is less clear. It may be the dusky bloom of her skin, which Arabic can call green, or simply the green of a garden in which the narcissus stands, so that the phrase makes a garden of her body; the reading is uncertain. The four nouns fall in rhyming pairs, al-narjis wa-al-khuḍra, bi-baṭnī wa-al-surra, with the rhyme in -ra, in the manner of rhymed prose. hārishnī and nāghishnī are imperatives of two Form III verbs of later Arabic, both of love-play, and they rhyme. hārasha is properly said of dogs snapping at one another, and in later use means to romp or play roughly with someone; nāghasha is to tease, flirt with, tickle. The exact shade of each is uncertain, but together they mean amorous play. ناغشنى has the edition's ى for final ي, though هارشني beside it has ي. bukra, “tomorrow”, is the everyday sense of a Classical word for “early morning”; it is pointed here without case, as it is said.

sentences.t: بِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ قُمْ يَا سَيِّدِي وَاتَّكِئْ عَلَى الْمِخَدَّةِ وَلَا تَنَمْ
sentences.tr: bi-Allāhi ʿalayka qum yā sayyidī wa-ittakiʾ ʿalā al-mikhaddati wa-lā tanam
sentences.l: By-God upon-you, rise, O my-master, and-recline on the-cushion, and-do-not sleep.
sentences.i: For God's sake, get up, my lord, lean back on the cushion, and do not sleep.”
sentences.n: bi-Allāhi ʿalayka, “by God, upon you”, is the same formula of adjuring as bi-ḥayātī ʿalayka. ittakaʾa ʿalā, Form VIII, “to recline, lean on”; its ئ is printed, as is the shadda of المخدّة. mikhadda, “cushion”, is the thing one lays the cheek (khadd) on. lā with the jussive forbids: lā tanam, “do not sleep”.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَرُدَّ عَلَيْهَا قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ جَوَابًا بَلْ غَطَّ فِى النَّوْمِ فَقَالَتْ يُوهْ يُوهْ أَنْتَ تَغْتَرُّ بِحُسْنِكَ وَجَمَالِكَ وَظَرْفِكَ وَدَلَالِكَ فَكَمَا أَنْتَ مَلِيحٌ أَنَا الْأُخْرَى أَيْضًا مَلِيحَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-lam yarudda ʿalayhā Qamaru al-Zamāni jawāban bal ghaṭṭa fī al-nawmi fa-qālat yūh yūh anta taghtarru bi-ḥusnika wa-jamālika wa-ẓarfika wa-dalālika fa-ka-mā anta malīḥun anā al-ukhrā ayḍan malīḥatun
sentences.l: But-not returned to-her Qamar al-Zamān an-answer; rather he-snored in the-sleep. And-she-said: Yūh, yūh! You, you-are-vain with-your-beauty and-your-loveliness and-your-elegance and-your-airs; so-as you (are) handsome, I the-other also (am) lovely.
sentences.i: But Qamar al-Zamān gave her no answer; he only snored on in his sleep. And she said, “Oh, oh! You are vain of your beauty and loveliness, your grace and your airs; and just as you are handsome, I too am lovely.
sentences.n: The print has خط, a misprint for غط, corrected here: ghaṭṭa fī al-nawmi, “he was sunk deep in sleep, he snored”; خ and غ both carry one dot, so this is a wrong letter, not a dropped dot. radda ʿalayhā jawāban, “returned her an answer”: ʿalā marks the one answered. فى is the edition's ى for final ي. yūh yūh is a cry of vexation or dismay from everyday speech, still heard in Egypt, and has no Classical form. ightarra bi-, Form VIII, “to be deluded by, vain of”: bi- marks what one is vain of; the shadda of تغترّ is the print's own. ẓarf is “elegance, grace”, and dalāl “coquetry”, the airs of a beloved who knows his worth; jamālika and dalālika rhyme. fa-ka-mā …, “so just as …”: “just as you are handsome, I too am lovely”. anā al-ukhrā, “I, the other”, means “I for my part”, a turn of later Arabic, with ukhrā, “other”, in the feminine to agree with the speaker.

sentences.t: فَمَا هٰذَا الَّذِي تَفْعَلُهُ هَلْ هُمْ عَلَّمُوكَ الصَّدَّ عَنِّى أَوْ أَبِي الشَّيْخُ النَّحْسُ عَلَّمَكَ وَمَنَعَكَ وَحَلَّفَكَ أَنَّكَ لَا تُكَلِّمُنِى هٰذِهِ اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-mā hādhā alladhī tafʿaluhu hal hum ʿallamūka al-ṣadda ʿannī aw abī al-shaykhu al-naḥsu ʿallamaka wa-manaʿaka wa-ḥallafaka annaka lā tukallimunī hādhihi al-laylata
sentences.l: So-what (is) this which you-are-doing? Did they teach-you the-turning-away from-me, or my-father, the-old-man, the-ill-omened, taught-you and-forbade-you and-made-you-swear that-you not speak-to-me this the-night?
sentences.i: What is this you are doing? Did they teach you to turn away from me? Or did my father, that ill-omened old man, teach you, and forbid you, and make you swear not to speak to me tonight?”
sentences.n: hal hum ʿallamūka, “did they teach you”: the subject pronoun hum stands before a verb that already carries it, an emphasis common in later Arabic. Budūr supposes that the young man was put into her bed by her father, angry at her refusals, and told to slight her. ṣadd, “turning away, aloofness”, is the lover's standing complaint; ʿan marks the one turned from. al-naḥs, “ill-omened”: she speaks of her father with open resentment. ḥallafa, Form II, “to make (someone) swear”; annaka lā tukallimunī, “that you will not speak to me”, gives what he swore. The shaddas of علّموك, الصدّ, عنّى, علّمك and حلّفك are printed, and عنّى and تكلمنى have the edition's ى for final ي.

sentences.t: فَمَا فَتَحَ قَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ فَمْ وَلَا انْتَبَهَ فَازْدَادَتْ فِيهِ مَحَبَّةً وَأَلْقَى اللَّهُ مَحَبَّتَهُ فِي قَلْبِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-mā fataḥa Qamaru al-Zamāni fam wa-lā intabaha fa-izdādat fīhi maḥabbatan wa-alqā Allāhu maḥabbatahu fī qalbihā
sentences.l: But-not opened Qamar al-Zamān a-mouth, nor woke; so-she-increased in-him (in) love, and-cast God love-of-him into her-heart.
sentences.i: But Qamar al-Zamān did not open his mouth, nor did he wake; and her love for him only grew, for God had cast love of him into her heart.
sentences.n: fataḥa fam, “to open a mouth”, is to say a word. The print sets فم without the alif of the accusative, where Classical Arabic would write faman; it is pointed here as it stands, without case, as it would be said. wa-lā intabaha, “nor did he wake”: lā with a perfect carries on the negation of mā. izdādat fīhi maḥabbatan, “she grew in love for him”: izdāda, Form VIII of zāda, “to increase”, with an accusative of specification, maḥabbatan, “in love”, and fī marking the one loved. maḥabbatahu, “love of him”: the pronoun is the one loved, not the one loving.

sentences.t: وَنَظَرَتْهُ نَظْرَةً أَعْقَبَتْهَا أَلْفُ حَسْرَةٍ فَخَفَقَ فُؤَادُهَا وَتَقَلْقَلَتْ أَحْشَاؤُهَا وَاضْطَرَبَتْ جَوَارِحُهَا
sentences.tr: wa-naẓarathu naẓratan aʿqabathā alfu ḥasratin fa-khafaqa fuʾāduhā wa-taqalqalat aḥshāʾuhā wa-iḍṭarabat jawāriḥuhā
sentences.l: And-she-looked-at-him a-look (that) followed-it a-thousand regrets; and-throbbed her-heart, and-were-shaken her-innards, and-trembled her-limbs.
sentences.i: She gave him one look, and a thousand sighs came after it; her heart throbbed, her insides were shaken, and her limbs trembled.
sentences.n: naẓarathu, “she looked at him”, takes its object directly, without ilā. naẓratan aʿqabathā alfu ḥasratin, “a look which a thousand regrets followed”: aʿqaba, Form IV, “to come after”, in a clause that describes the indefinite naẓratan without a relative pronoun; the verb is feminine by attraction to ḥasra, though its subject is alf. ḥasra, “regret, a sigh of longing”. Three verbs then run through the body's distress, and the three subjects rhyme in -uhā: khafaqa, “to throb”; taqalqala, a quadriliteral, “to be shaken, unsettled”; iḍṭaraba, Form VIII, “to be agitated, tremble”. jawāriḥ, “limbs”, the body's working members. The ؤ of فؤادها and of احشاؤها is printed.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِقَمَرِ الزَّمَانِ يَا سَيِّدِي كَلِّمْنِى يَا حَبِيبِي حَدِّثْنِى يَا مَعْشُوقِي رُدَّ عَلَيَّ الْجَوَابَ وَقُلْ لِي مَا اسْمُكَ فَإِنَّكَ قَدْ سَلَبْتَ عَقْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-qālat li-Qamari al-Zamāni yā sayyidī kallimnī yā ḥabībī ḥaddithnī yā maʿshūqī rudda ʿalayya al-jawāba wa-qul lī mā ismuka fa-innaka qad salabta ʿaqlī
sentences.l: And-she-said to-Qamar al-Zamān: O my-master, speak-to-me; O my-darling, talk-to-me; O my-beloved, return to-me the-answer, and-say to-me what (is) your-name, for-indeed-you have robbed my-mind.
sentences.i: And she said to Qamar al-Zamān, “My lord, speak to me; my darling, talk to me; my beloved, give me an answer, and tell me your name, for you have robbed me of my wits.”
sentences.n: The print has لقمر الرمان, a misprint for لقمر الزمان, corrected here: li-Qamari al-Zamāni, the dot of the zāy having dropped. li-, “to”, marks the one spoken to. The calls run in pairs, yā sayyidī kallimnī, yā ḥabībī ḥaddithnī, yā maʿshūqī …; the imperatives كلّمنى and حدّثنى carry the print's own shadda and the edition's ى for final ي. maʿshūq, “beloved”, is the passive participle of ʿashiqa, “to love passionately”. rudda ʿalayya al-jawāba, “give the answer back to me”: ʿalā marks the one answered, and the shaddas of ردّ and عليّ are printed. mā ismuka, “what is your name?”: the alif of ism is not pronounced after mā. salaba, “to rob”: salabta ʿaqlī, “you have stolen my reason”.

sentences.t: كُلُّ ذٰلِكَ وَقَمَرُ الزَّمَانِ مُسْتَغْرِقٌ فِى النَّوْمِ وَلَمْ يَرُدَّ عَلَيْهَا بِكَلِمَةٍ
sentences.tr: kullu dhālika wa-Qamaru al-Zamāni mustaghriqun fī al-nawmi wa-lam yarudda ʿalayhā bi-kalimatin
sentences.l: All that, and-Qamar al-Zamān (was) sunk in the-sleep, and-not he-returned to-her with-a-word.
sentences.i: All this while Qamar al-Zamān lay sunk in sleep, and did not answer her a word.
sentences.n: kullu dhālika wa-…, “all that, while …”: kullu dhālika stands on its own, “(all) that (happened)”, and wa- brings in a circumstantial clause. istaghraqa, Form X, “to be sunk, absorbed”: mustaghriq fī al-nawm, “drowned in sleep”. radda ʿalayhā bi-kalimatin, “answered her with a word”: bi- marks the word given back. فى has the edition's ى for final ي.

sentences.t: فَتَأَوَّهَتِ الْمَلِكَةُ بُدُورُ وَقَالَتْ لَهُ يُوهْ يُوهْ مَالَكَ مُعْجَبًا بِنَفْسِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-taʾawwahati al-malikatu Budūru wa-qālat lahu yūh yūh mā laka muʿjaban bi-nafsika
sentences.l: And-sighed the-Queen Budūr and-said to-him: Yūh, yūh! What (is) to-you, pleased with-yourself?
sentences.i: Queen Budūr sighed and said to him, “Oh, oh! What ails you, that you are so taken with yourself?
sentences.n: taʾawwaha, Form V, “to say āh, to sigh”; the hamza of فتأوهت is printed. yūh yūh is again the everyday cry of vexation. mā laka, “what is to you?”, that is, “what is the matter with you?”, is printed as one word, مالك. muʿjaban bi-nafsika, “pleased with yourself”, is a circumstantial accusative: “what ails you, (being) so pleased with yourself?”. muʿjab bi-, passive participle of aʿjaba, Form IV, “pleased with, taken with”: bi- marks what one admires.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ هَزَّتْهُ وَقَلَّبَتْ يَدَهُ فَرَأَتْ خَاتَمَهَا فِي إِصْبَعِهِ الْخِنْصَرِ فَشَهَقَتْ شَهْقَةً وَأَتْبَعَتْهَا بِغَنْجَةٍ وَقَالَتْ أَوَّاهْ أَوَّاهْ
sentences.tr: thumma hazzathu wa-qallabat yadahu fa-raʾat khātamahā fī iṣbaʿihi al-khinṣiri fa-shahaqat shahqatan wa-atbaʿathā bi-ghanjatin wa-qālat awwāh awwāh
sentences.l: Then she-shook-him and-turned-over his-hand, and-saw her-ring on his-finger, the-little-finger; and-she-gasped a-gasp and-followed-it with-a-coo, and-said: Awwāh, awwāh!
sentences.i: Then she shook him and turned his hand over, and saw her own ring on his little finger; and she gasped, and after the gasp gave a languishing coo, and said, “Ah me, ah me!
sentences.n: The shaddas of هزّته and قلّبت are printed; qallaba, Form II, “to turn over”. iṣbaʿihi al-khinṣiri, “his finger, the little finger”: khinṣir, “little finger”, stands in apposition to iṣbaʿ, where Classical usage would simply say khinṣirihi, “his little finger”. Arabic puts a ring “in” (fī) a finger. This is the ring Qamar al-Zamān drew off her finger while she slept, in the last night. shahaqa, “to gasp”, with its cognate accusative shahqatan. ghanja, “a coy, languishing murmur”, from ghunj, “coquetry”. atbaʿa bi-, Form IV, “to follow (one thing) with (another)”: bi- marks what comes after. awwāh, a cry of pain or longing, “ah!”; the shadda is printed, and the word is pointed here in pause.

sentences.t: وَاللَّهِ أَنْتَ حَبِيبِي وَتُحِبُّنِي وَلٰكِنْ كَأَنَّكَ تُعْرِضُ عَنِّي دَلَالًا مَعَ أَنَّكَ يَا حَبِيبِي جِئْتَنِي وَأَنَا نَائِمَةٌ وَمَا أَعْرِفُ مَا فَعَلْتَ مَعِي وَأَخَذْتَ خَاتَمِي وَلٰكِنْ مَا أَنَا قَالِعَةٌ خَاتَمِي مِنْ إِصْبَعِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-Allāhi anta ḥabībī wa-tuḥibbunī wa-lākin ka-annaka tuʿriḍu ʿannī dalālan maʿa annaka yā ḥabībī jiʾtanī wa-anā nāʾimatun wa-mā aʿrifu mā faʿalta maʿī wa-akhadhta khātamī wa-lākin mā anā qāliʿatun khātamī min iṣbaʿika
sentences.l: By-God, you (are) my-beloved and-you-love-me; but as-though-you turn-away from-me (out of) coquetry, although you, O my-beloved, came-to-me while-I (was) sleeping, and-not I-know what you-did with-me, and-you-took my-ring. But not I (am) taking-off my-ring from your-finger.
sentences.i: By God, you are my beloved and you love me, and yet you seem to turn away from me out of coquetry, though you came to me, my darling, while I was asleep, did with me I know not what, and took my ring. But I will not take my ring off your finger.”
sentences.n: ka-annaka, “as though you”, is printed كانك, with bare alif, as the edition almost always prints alif without hamza. aʿraḍa ʿan, Form IV, “to turn away from”; dalālan, “out of coquetry”, is an accusative of cause. The shadda of عنّي is printed. maʿa anna, “although”, literally “with (the fact) that”. wa-anā nāʾimatun, “while I was asleep”: wa- brings in a circumstantial clause. The ئ of جئتني and of نائمة is printed. mā aʿrifu mā faʿalta maʿī, “I do not know what you did with me”: the first mā denies, the second asks. In mā anā qāliʿatun, “I am not taking off”, qalaʿa, properly “to uproot”, is the ordinary later word for taking off a garment or a ring, and the active participle stands for an intention, “I am not going to take off”, a use common in later Arabic. After mā the Classical grammar of the Ḥijāz would put the predicate in the accusative, qāliʿatan; the nominative is the other, Tamīmī, usage, and that of speech. She leaves her ring on his finger; what she takes instead comes below.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ فَتَحَتْ جَيْبَ قَمِيصِهِ وَمَالَتْ عَلَيْهِ فَقَبَّلَتْهُ وَمَدَّتْ يَدَهَا إِلَيْهِ تُفَتِّشُهُ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ تَرَى مَعَهُ شَيْأً تَأْخُذُهُ فَلَمْ تَجِدْ شَيْأً
sentences.tr: thumma fataḥat jayba qamīṣihi wa-mālat ʿalayhi fa-qabbalathu wa-maddat yadahā ilayhi tufattishuhu li-ajli an tarā maʿahu shayʾan taʾkhudhuhu fa-lam tajid shayʾan
sentences.l: Then she-opened (the) neck-opening (of) his-shirt and-leaned over-him and-kissed-him, and-stretched-out her-hand to-him, searching-him, for-the-sake that she-see with-him a-thing she-takes-it; but-not she-found a-thing.
sentences.i: Then she opened the neck of his shirt, bent over him and kissed him, and put out her hand to him, searching him to see whether he had anything on him that she might take; but she found nothing.
sentences.n: jayb, “the neck-opening of a garment”, the slit at the breast. māla ʿalā, “to lean over”. فقبلته is printed without the shadda the word carries elsewhere in this night: qabbala, Form II, “to kiss”. tufattishuhu, “searching him”, is a circumstantial imperfect: fattasha, Form II, “to search”, with its shadda printed. li-ajli an, “in order that”, takes the subjunctive tarā. maʿahu, “with him”, here means “on him”. shayʾan taʾkhudhuhu, “a thing she might take”: the verb describes the indefinite noun without a relative pronoun. شيأ is the edition's spelling of shayʾan, with the hamza printed on the alif of the accusative, where Classical spelling has شيئا.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَتْ بِيَدِهَا إِلَى صَدْرِهَا فَزَلِقَتْ يَدُهَا مِنْ نُعُومَةِ جِسْمِهِ إِلَى بَطْنِهِ فَنَزَلَتْ إِلَى سُرَّتِهِ فَسَقَطَتْ يَدُهَا عَلَى أَيْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-nazalat bi-yadihā ilā ṣadrihā fa-zaliqat yaduhā min nuʿūmati jismihi ilā baṭnihi fa-nazalat ilā surratihi fa-saqaṭat yaduhā ʿalā ayrihi
sentences.l: And-she-went-down with-her-hand to her-chest; and-slipped her-hand from (the) smoothness (of) his-body to his-belly, and-it-went-down to his-navel, and-fell her-hand upon his-penis.
sentences.i: She moved her hand down to his chest, and so smooth was his body that her hand slid down to his belly; it went on down to his navel, and came to rest on his penis.
sentences.n: صدرها is doubtful. As printed it is ṣadrihā, “her chest”, and it is pointed so here, but the sense seems to want ṣadrihi, “his chest”, since her hand is searching his body and slides on from there to his belly; the idiomatic rendering follows that sense. nazalat bi-yadihā, “she went down with her hand”: bi- marks what is brought down. zaliqa, “to slip”; min nuʿūmati jismihi, “from the smoothness of his body”: min gives the cause. The second fa-nazalat has her hand (yad, feminine) as its subject. ayr, “penis”, is the plain word, and the narrator uses it without comment.

sentences.t: فَانْصَدَعَ قَلْبُهَا وَارْتَجَفَ فُؤَادُهَا وَهَاجَتْ عَلَيْهَا الشَّهْوَةُ لِأَنَّ شَهْوَةَ النِّسَاءِ أَقْوَى مِنْ شَهْوَةِ الرِّجَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-inṣadaʿa qalbuhā wa-irtajafa fuʾāduhā wa-hājat ʿalayhā al-shahwatu li-anna shahwata al-nisāʾi aqwā min shahwati al-rijāli
sentences.l: And-was-cracked her-heart, and-quaked her-heart, and-surged upon-her the-desire, because (the) desire (of) the-women (is) stronger than (the) desire (of) the-men.
sentences.i: Her heart was split and shaken, and desire surged up in her; for the desire of women is stronger than the desire of men.
sentences.n: inṣadaʿa, Form VII, “to be cracked, split”; irtajafa, Form VIII, “to quake”; the ؤ of فؤادها is printed. qalb and fuʾād both mean “heart”, fuʾād being the more inward and poetic word. hājat ʿalayhā al-shahwatu, “desire surged upon her”: hāja, “to be stirred up, rage”, with ʿalā marking the one overcome. The closing maxim, that women's desire is stronger than men's, is a commonplace the Nights repeats more than once; the narrator offers it as a matter of course.

sentences.t: فَخَجِلَتْ ثُمَّ نَزَعَتْ خَاتَمَهُ مِنْ إِصْبَعِهِ وَوَضَعَتْهُ فِي إِصْبَعِهَا عِوَضًا عَنْ خَاتَمِهَا وَقَبَّلَتْهُ فِي ثَغْرِهِ وَقَبَّلَتْ كَفَّيْهِ وَلَمْ تَتْرُكْ فِيهِ مَوْضِعًا إِلَّا قَبَّلَتْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-khajilat thumma nazaʿat khātamahu min iṣbaʿihi wa-waḍaʿathu fī iṣbaʿihā ʿiwaḍan ʿan khātamihā wa-qabbalathu fī thaghrihi wa-qabbalat kaffayhi wa-lam tatruk fīhi mawḍiʿan illā qabbalathu
sentences.l: And-she-was-abashed; then she-drew-off his-ring from his-finger and-put-it on her-finger in-exchange for her-ring, and-kissed-him on his-mouth, and-kissed his-two-palms, and-not she-left on-him a-place except she-kissed-it.
sentences.i: She was abashed; then she drew his ring off his finger and put it on her own in place of hers, and kissed him on the mouth, and kissed his palms, and left no part of him that she did not kiss.
sentences.n: The print has موصغا, a misprint for موضعا, corrected here: mawḍiʿan, “a place”, with the dot of the ḍād dropped and a stray dot over the ʿayn. khajila, “to be abashed”, at her own desire. nazaʿa, “to pull off”. fī iṣbaʿihā, “on her finger”: Arabic puts a ring “in” a finger. ʿiwaḍan ʿan, “in exchange for, in place of”: an accusative used adverbially, with ʿan marking what is replaced. thaghr, properly the front teeth, is “mouth” in the language of love. kaffayhi, “his two palms”, a dual. The shaddas of كفّيه and of both قبّلته are printed, while وقبلت is printed without one. lam tatruk fīhi mawḍiʿan illā qabbalathu, “she left no place on him but she kissed it”: negation with illā makes it “every place”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَعْدَ ذٰلِكَ تَقَدَّمَتْ إِلَيْهِ وَأَخَذَتْهُ فِي حِضْنِهَا وَعَانَقَتْهُ وَوَضَعَتْ إِحْدَى يَدَيْهَا تَحْتَ رَقَبَتِهِ وَالْأُخْرَى مِنْ تَحْتِ إِبْطِهِ وَاعْتَنَقَتْهُ وَنَامَتْ بِجَانِبِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma baʿda dhālika taqaddamat ilayhi wa-akhadhathu fī ḥiḍnihā wa-ʿānaqathu wa-waḍaʿat iḥdā yadayhā taḥta raqabatihi wa-al-ukhrā min taḥti ibṭihi wa-iʿtanaqathu wa-nāmat bi-jānibihi
sentences.l: Then after that she-came-forward to-him and-took-him into her-bosom and-embraced-him, and-put one (of) her-two-hands under his-neck and-the-other from under his-armpit, and-clasped-him, and-slept at-his-side.
sentences.i: After that she drew close to him, took him in her arms and embraced him; she put one hand under his neck and the other under his arm, held him close, and fell asleep beside him.
sentences.n: taqaddama ilā, Form V, “to come forward to”; the shadda of تقدّمت is printed. ḥiḍn, “bosom, embrace”: akhadhathu fī ḥiḍnihā, “she took him into her arms”. ʿānaqa, Form III, and iʿtanaqa, Form VIII, both mean “to embrace”, from ʿunuq, “neck”: the narrator plays on one root. iḥdā, “one”, is feminine to agree with yad, “hand”, as is al-ukhrā, “the other”. min taḥti ibṭihi, “from under his armpit”. nāmat bi-jānibihi, “she slept at his side”, answers Qamar al-Zamān in the last night, who took her ring, turned his back on her and slept: each has now taken the other's ring, but she sleeps holding him.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the-morning overtook Shahrazād, and-she-fell-silent from the-permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The closing formula, as at the end of every night.
